summary: Specifies the Group Domain of Interpretation, a protocol that manages keys for groups of devices so they can communicate securely, for example with IPsec. A group controller hands out the keys and security associations to members. This version replaces RFC 3547, and it was in turn replaced by RFC 9838.

plainLanguage.summary: If a whole class must share a secret code, someone has to hand it out safely and change it when needed. GDOI is the system that hands a group the same key. It replaced an older one and was later replaced itself.

questions: how does multicast key distribution work
subtitle: Protocol for a group controller to distribute keys to members of a secure group.

tldr.problem: Secure multicast and group communications require all members to share the same keys and security policies. A single centralized server must be able to hand out keys securely, revoke membership by refusing to rekey departing members, and update policy for all members at once.
tldr.mechanism: GDOI defines two message exchanges: GROUPKEY-PULL, in which a group member requests keys from a Group Controller/Key Server (GCKS), and GROUPKEY-PUSH, in which the GCKS sends key updates to all members. Both are protected by ISAKMP Phase 1 for authentication. A Rekey SA protects the GROUPKEY-PUSH messages; a Key Encryption Key and Traffic Encryption Key distribute actual group keys.
tldr.outcome: Groups can securely coordinate with a single key server, support membership changes without rekeying the entire group, and deliver confidential multicast traffic. It replaced RFC 3547 and was in turn replaced by RFC 9838.

facts.label: Phase 1 requirement
facts.value: MUST be protected by ISAKMP Phase 1

facts.label: Rekey SA protection
facts.value: GROUPKEY-PUSH messages are protected by a symmetric Key Encrypting Key

today: This RFC replaced RFC 3547 with updated clarifications and corrections. It was superseded by RFC 9838 in 2020, which further refined GDOI for modern multicast security architectures.

sections.title: Group Key Management Architecture
sections.content:
GDOI is a Domain of Interpretation (DOI) for ISAKMP that manages group security associations. In the GDOI model, there is one trusted Group Controller/Key Server (GCKS) and multiple Group Members (GMs). GMs register with the GCKS to join the group, and the GCKS distributes keys and policies that allow the group members to communicate securely.

Unlike pairwise key exchange (where each pair of peers negotiates keys), GDOI uses a centralized key distribution model. All GMs in a group receive the same keys from the GCKS. This simplifies group policy: the GCKS can change the keys for everyone without negotiating with each member individually. GMs learn about key changes either by pulling (requesting) or by having the GCKS push updates to them.

GDOI defines security associations for two purposes: a Rekey SA protects the GROUPKEY-PUSH messages from the GCKS, and Data-Security SAs describe the actual traffic (e.g., IPsec) that the group uses.
sections.plainLanguage: GDOI is like a secret club with one boss (the GCKS) and many members. When you want to join, you ask the boss "can I be in your club?" The boss checks that you are legitimate, gives you the secret password for this week, and tells you the rules ("messages go to 224.1.1.1 and use AES encryption"). Later, the boss might send a broadcast message saying "new password is now XYZABC."

sections.title: Two-Phase Security
sections.content:
GDOI uses the ISAKMP two-phase model. Phase 1 establishes mutual authentication between the GM and GCKS over a secure, encrypted channel. The GM proves its identity using certificates or other authentication, and the GCKS verifies that the GM is authorized. Phase 1 negotiation uses standard ISAKMP procedures (identity protection exchanges, digital signatures) and produces a Phase 1 SA that protects subsequent traffic.

Phase 2 is the GROUPKEY-PULL exchange, which runs inside the Phase 1 SA. The GM sends a request for group keys, the GCKS responds with the keys and policies, and the GM installs them. Unlike Phase 1 (which requires mutual negotiation), Phase 2 is a simple request-response: the GCKS decides what keys to send, and the GM accepts them or leaves the group.
sections.plainLanguage: Phase 1 is like showing your membership card at the club door. Phase 2 is like asking the boss for this week's secret password and the club rules. You need to pass Phase 1 before you can do Phase 2.

sections.title: GROUPKEY-PULL Exchange
sections.content:
The GROUPKEY-PULL exchange is a four-message exchange between a GM and GCKS. Message 1 (from GM): the GM sends a Hash, a Nonce (random value), and its Group ID (which group it wants to join). Message 2 (from GCKS): the GCKS responds with a Hash, a Nonce, and a Security Association payload describing the group's policies (which algorithms to use, which keys to distribute). Message 3 (from GM): the GM acknowledges and optionally requests resources (e.g., buffer space) with a Group Associated Policy payload. Message 4 (from GCKS): the GCKS sends the actual keys in a Key Download payload, and optionally the current sequence number in a Sequence Number payload.

The Sequence Number prevents replay attacks on GROUPKEY-PUSH updates. When a new GM joins, it receives the current sequence number; it will reject any GROUPKEY-PUSH message with a lower or equal sequence number, preventing an attacker from replaying old key updates.
sections.plainLanguage: GROUPKEY-PULL is like a four-step conversation: GM says "hi, I want to join group SPORTS"; GCKS says "ok, here is what we use for SPORTS"; GM says "got it, I have space for the keys"; GCKS says "here are the keys, use version 42 of them."

sections.title: GROUPKEY-PUSH Rekey Messages
sections.content:
The GROUPKEY-PUSH exchange is initiated by the GCKS to distribute new keys to the group. Unlike GROUPKEY-PULL (initiated by the GM), GROUPKEY-PUSH is initiated and pushed by the server. GROUPKEY-PUSH messages are typically sent as a datagram to a multicast address, so all group members receive them at once. Each GROUPKEY-PUSH message is protected by the Rekey SA (a symmetric key that all GMs share), not by ISAKMP Phase 1.

A GROUPKEY-PUSH message contains new keys and policies that update the group's Data-Security SAs. It also increments the sequence number, allowing members to detect if they missed a push message. The GCKS can use GROUPKEY-PUSH to distribute updated Traffic Encryption Keys (refreshing the actual data protection keys), update IPsec policies, or even revoke membership by not sending updates to departing members.
sections.plainLanguage: GROUPKEY-PUSH is like the boss sending a broadcast message to everyone in the club saying "new secret password is ABCXYZ, and we have a new rule about meeting times." Everyone who got this message can now use the new password; anyone who missed it will not be able to decrypt group messages.

sections.title: Key Types and Group Policy
sections.content:
GDOI manages two types of keys. The Key Encrypting Key (KEK) protects the GROUPKEY-PUSH messages themselves. All group members share the same KEK, allowing them to decrypt rekey messages from the server. The KEK is delivered in the GROUPKEY-PULL exchange. The Traffic Encryption Key (TEK) is the actual key used to encrypt group traffic (e.g., IPsec ESP packets). The GCKS distributes the TEK(s) inside the protected GROUPKEY-PULL and GROUPKEY-PUSH messages.

The Group Associated Policy (GAP) payload specifies additional group properties such as the active Group Member list (for forward and backward access control), activation time delays (when new members can start sending), and deactivation delays (when removed members stop receiving). This allows the GCKS to control when new members may join or when removed members are no longer able to decrypt group traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: The KEK is the key to the locked mailbox where the boss puts new passwords. The TEK is the actual password members use for their secret messages. When the boss adds a new person to the club, the boss can set a delay so the new person cannot talk for 5 minutes (giving time to announce the new member), and old members are blocked after 1 minute (so they cannot spy on the new passwords).

sections.title: Security Properties and Considerations
sections.content:
GDOI achieves several security goals. Forward access control (backward secrecy) ensures that members who leave the group cannot decrypt future messages: when a member is removed, the GCKS distributes a new KEK and TEK to all remaining members via GROUPKEY-PUSH, and the departing member cannot decrypt it (since it does not have the old KEK to decrypt the update). Backward access control (forward secrecy) prevents a newly joined member from decrypting past messages: the GCKS does not send old keys to new members, only current and future keys.

GMs must authenticate the GCKS to prevent rogue servers from distributing false keys. The Phase 1 SA provides this authentication. The GCKS should authenticate GMs before allowing them to join. Replay protection via sequence numbers prevents an attacker from replaying old GROUPKEY-PUSH messages. The Rekey SA (a symmetric key) protects the GROUPKEY-PUSH messages themselves; if an attacker could forge these messages, it could send false keys to the group. Therefore, the Rekey SA MUST be securely distributed in Phase 2.
sections.plainLanguage: When Alice leaves the club, the boss sends a new password (encrypted with the old mailbox key) to everyone else. Alice cannot read it because she left, so she does not learn the new password and cannot decrypt new club messages. When Bob joins, the boss does not give him the old passwords, so he cannot read messages sent before he joined. An attacker trying to trick the club with a fake password will fail because the fake message is not encrypted with the real mailbox key.

messages.label: HDR*, HASH(1), Ni, ID
messages.note: Member requests SPORTS group using a nonce and identity.

messages.label: HDR*, HASH(2), Nr, SA
messages.note: Server acknowledges, sends group security association and its nonce.

messages.label: HDR*, HASH(3) [,GAP]
messages.note: Member confirms receipt; optionally requests resources or policy.

messages.label: HDR*, HASH(4), [SEQ,] KD
messages.note: Server sends current sequence number and key download with KEK and TEK.

viz.caption: Pull vs. Push: Two Modes of Key Distribution

left.title: GROUPKEY-PULL
left.desc: Member asks for keys. Four messages. Protected by Phase 1 SA. Used for initial registration.

right.title: GROUPKEY-PUSH
right.desc: Server pushes updates to group. One or two messages. Protected by Rekey SA. Used for rekeying all members.
